facts.claim: HarperCollins states that the revised edition added two new chapters.
facts.mechanism: Because the publisher metadata explains why accidental Diminisher material belongs to the revised edition.
facts.commonError: Assuming accidental diminishing was necessarily part of the original 2010 release.
facts.whyWrong: The public revised-edition page specifically names added chapters.

facts.claim: One added revised-edition topic is accidental Diminishers.
facts.mechanism: Because the added topic turns the model toward self-diagnosis by well-intentioned leaders.
facts.commonError: Thinking only openly controlling leaders can diminish people.
facts.whyWrong: Well-intentioned leaders can reduce contribution through impact rather than motive.

facts.claim: Another added revised-edition topic is how to deal with Diminishers.
facts.mechanism: Because the revised close includes both self-diagnosis and tactics for people experiencing diminishing behavior.
facts.commonError: Merging accidental diminishing with coping tactics as the same lesson.
facts.whyWrong: One topic diagnoses one's own habits; the other addresses working under someone else.

facts.claim: Google Project Oxygen treated manager effectiveness as observable behavior.
facts.mechanism: Because behavior-based diagnosis makes accidental diminishing visible even when intention is positive.
facts.commonError: Judging manager quality only by what the manager meant to do.
facts.whyWrong: Impact appears in repeated behaviors and team experience.

facts.claim: Project Oxygen is a Google manager-research case.
facts.mechanism: Because the case gives the diagnostic idea a concrete organization and named project.
facts.commonError: Using unnamed management research as generic proof.
facts.whyWrong: The project name and company make the case checkable.

facts.claim: Radical Candor pairs care personally with challenge directly.
facts.mechanism: Because the two-part frame shows that good leadership impact requires more than one positive intention.
facts.commonError: Assuming care alone is enough to grow people.
facts.whyWrong: Care without challenge can protect people from growth; challenge without care can become threat.

facts.claim: Accidental diminishing is defined by impact rather than malicious motive.
facts.mechanism: Because people can be crowded out by helpful over-functioning, the absence of bad intent does not guarantee good effect.
facts.commonError: Waiting to change until someone proves bad intent.
facts.whyWrong: Leadership impact can be harmful without malicious intent.

facts.claim: Rescuing too quickly can be an accidental diminishing pattern.
facts.mechanism: Because quick rescue takes the problem back before people finish building judgment and ownership.
facts.whyWrong: Support that removes the hard thinking can reduce future capability.

facts.claim: A useful repair starts with one observable behavior, not a full personality rewrite.
facts.mechanism: Because replacing a repeatable habit gives the team a visible difference and lowers defensiveness for the leader.
facts.commonError: Trying to become a completely different person overnight.
facts.whyWrong: Broad identity change is harder to sustain than one specific behavior change.

allowedAnchors.label: accidental diminishing
allowedAnchors.text: Accidental diminishing occurs when a leader intends to help, inspire, or move quickly but behaves in ways that crowd out other people's thinking. The harm comes from impact, not motive. Readers gain a less defensive route into change. Instead of deciding whether they are bad leaders, they can inspect repeatable habits that unintentionally reduce contribution.
